frictionVectors.title: European energy dependence
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong control through Sonatrach, but European buyers seek diversified supplies and greater contract flexibility. Long-term gas demand uncertainty pressures future investment.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel and Western Sahara exposure
frictionVectors.details: Instability across southern borders and rivalry with Morocco complicate transport, security, and regional energy diplomacy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-financed infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: The Lobito Corridor attracts US, European, and Gulf interest because of its access to Central African minerals. Angola can capture transit value, but external financing and operators may limit domestic control.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: State revenues remain heavily exposed to oil prices, declining production, and foreign technical capital. Diversification has advanced slowly relative to resource dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou trade vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Benin is expanding port and logistics capacity, but trade remains sensitive to border politics with Nigeria and regional supply-chain shifts.

frictionVectors.title: Northern insurgency spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and militant infiltration from Burkina Faso and Niger threaten transport corridors, protected areas, and northern agricultural production.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond-market dependence
frictionVectors.details: Botswana has strengthened domestic value capture and negotiated a larger share of diamond production, but remains exposed to weak global demand and synthetic-stone competition.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure diversification gap
frictionVectors.details: Limited rail, power, and export connectivity constrain expansion beyond diamonds. New minerals and renewable projects require substantial external capital and regional transport coordination.

frictionVectors.title: Mining-sector renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: Authorities are seeking greater state participation and domestic processing in gold, challenging established foreign operators. Production and revenues remain vulnerable to insecurity and informal extraction.

frictionVectors.title: Security-for-influence tradeoff
frictionVectors.details: The government’s break with Western security partners and closer ties with Russia increase political autonomy but complicate access to finance, technology, and accountable infrastructure support.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern DRC Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Burundi's security posture is increasingly tied to instability in eastern DRC and its tense relationship with Rwanda. Cross-border armed-group activity and competing regional alignments constrain Bujumbura's strategic autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining and Finance
frictionVectors.details: The government seeks greater control over nickel and other mineral projects but remains dependent on foreign capital, infrastructure, and commodity markets. Limited fiscal capacity weakens its negotiating position with external investors.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime Security and Illegal Fishing
frictionVectors.details: Cabo Verde's large maritime zone is strategically valuable but costly to monitor. Illegal fishing, trafficking, and reliance on foreign surveillance and naval assistance limit full sovereign control over offshore resources.

frictionVectors.title: Competing Port and Airfield Partnerships
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investment in ports, airports, digital networks, and maritime facilities provides revenue and connectivity while creating exposure to competition among European, Chinese, and other external actors.

highlights: Oil, Gas, and Timber Under Pressure

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone Conflict and Infrastructure Risk
frictionVectors.details: Separatist violence in the Northwest and Southwest continues to threaten roads, plantations, energy assets, and state authority. The conflict also creates openings for foreign commercial and security actors to negotiate around central institutions.

frictionVectors.title: External Control of Strategic Corridors
frictionVectors.details: Oil, gas, timber, mining, and transport projects rely heavily on foreign operators and lenders, including Chinese-backed infrastructure. Cameroon retains formal ownership but captures uneven value and faces limited transparency over major concessions.

highlights: State Authority Beyond the Capital Remains Thin

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security and Mining Presence
frictionVectors.details: The government's reliance on Russian-linked security personnel has strengthened regime protection but deepened dependence on an external partner. Security cooperation is closely associated with access to gold and diamond networks, reducing transparency and public resource capture.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan and Chad Border Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Conflict and trafficking across the Sudanese and Chadian borders strain humanitarian corridors and state control over frontier resources. Armed groups and informal traders continue to compete with government institutions for territory and revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan Conflict and Refugee Influx
frictionVectors.details: The war in Sudan is intensifying pressure on Chad's eastern provinces through refugee flows, arms trafficking, and cross-border ethnic and political ties. This diverts state resources and increases dependence on external security and humanitarian support.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Energy and Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Oil production and export infrastructure remain dependent on foreign operators, technical systems, and transit arrangements, while security cooperation with outside powers shapes access to strategic corridors. N'Djamena retains political control but has limited ability to diversify revenue or infrastructure ownership.

frictionVectors.title: French control of Mayotte
frictionVectors.details: France retains control of Mayotte, sustaining a core sovereignty dispute and limiting Comoros' effective maritime jurisdiction. The issue remains politically potent and complicates cooperation on migration and security.

frictionVectors.title: External dependence and limited connectivity
frictionVectors.details: Comoros relies heavily on remittances, foreign aid, and imported fuel while infrastructure investment remains fragmented. Gulf, French, and other external partners have influence disproportionate to the country's domestic bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and state-backed investors retain major influence over copper and cobalt production, refining, and logistics. Kinshasa is seeking better contract terms and local processing but remains constrained by financing and technical dependence.

frictionVectors.title: M23, Rwanda, and eastern corridors
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the east continues to weaken state control over territory, mining zones, and transport routes. Regional military involvement and illicit mineral flows undermine Kinshasa's sovereignty despite diplomatic and security efforts.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon dependence
frictionVectors.details: The state remains highly dependent on offshore oil revenues and foreign operators, leaving public finances exposed to production and price volatility. Limited diversification reduces the government's leverage over external capital.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure influence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese financing and construction have expanded roads and other infrastructure while increasing long-term exposure to creditor and contractor interests. Transparency and repayment concerns constrain sovereign control over strategic projects.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign dominance of cocoa value chains
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is a leading cocoa producer, but processing, branding, and downstream margins remain heavily controlled by international firms. Government efforts to raise farm incomes and expand domestic processing are improving leverage gradually.

frictionVectors.title: Northern security and regional spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and instability in the Sahel continue to pressure northern border communities and security budgets. External military and development partnerships remain important, though Abidjan retains comparatively strong institutional control.

frictionVectors.title: Competing foreign military presence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti monetizes its position through U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military facilities, but this dependence limits independent strategic maneuver. Rival powers' proximity raises the risk that local infrastructure becomes tied to wider confrontation.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed port and rail projects have expanded connectivity while creating debt, utilization, and governance pressures. Ethiopia's reliance on Djibouti's corridors gives Djibouti leverage, but also makes national revenue highly exposed to regional trade and political shocks.

frictionVectors.title: GERD Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to view Ethiopia’s dam operations as a strategic threat to Nile flows. Negotiations remain vulnerable to unilateral filling and broader regional tensions.

frictionVectors.title: External Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF programs, Gulf investment, and multilateral support stabilize Egypt’s finances but increase outside influence over major assets, exchange-rate policy, and infrastructure priorities.

frictionVectors.title: Maturing Oil and Gas Fields
frictionVectors.details: Falling legacy production is pushing Malabo toward new offshore investment and gas monetization. Foreign operators retain substantial technical and financial leverage over the sector.

frictionVectors.title: China-Linked Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure projects and lending relationships with Chinese firms support connectivity but can deepen debt, opacity, and external influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Regional Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s coastline gives it leverage amid competition involving Ethiopia, Gulf states, Egypt, and other Red Sea actors. Port development remains constrained by sanctions risk, diplomatic isolation, and limited capital.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Mining
frictionVectors.details: Copper, gold, and zinc projects provide export revenue but rely heavily on foreign operators and financing. Revenue concentration limits broader domestic control over mineral value chains.

frictionVectors.title: Cross-Border Infrastructure Reliance
frictionVectors.details: Eswatini depends heavily on South African transport corridors, electricity markets, trade routes, and investment. Any regional disruption or political friction would quickly affect domestic resource security.

frictionVectors.title: Limited Economic Diversification
frictionVectors.details: Sugar, forestry, textiles, and remittances remain exposed to external markets and preferential access arrangements. Sovereign bargaining power is constrained by the small domestic market.

frictionVectors.title: Nile Basin Confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam strengthens Ethiopia’s electricity and bargaining position but remains a central source of tension with Egypt and Sudan over filling, operations, and downstream guarantees.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and the search for port access expose Addis Ababa to pressure from Gulf states, China, Gulf of Aden actors, and international financial institutions. Internal conflict also threatens transport and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign oil leverage
frictionVectors.details: The transitional-to-elected government is seeking greater national participation and domestic processing in hydrocarbons, but Gabon remains dependent on foreign operators, capital, and technical expertise.

frictionVectors.title: Railway and manganese bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Manganese exports remain vulnerable to rail and port constraints, limiting Libreville's ability to capture more value from its mineral base.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign fishing access
frictionVectors.details: Weak maritime enforcement leaves Gambian waters exposed to illegal, underreported, and foreign-controlled fishing, reducing the country's effective control over a major resource.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Gambia's transport, energy, and food-security systems remain closely tied to Senegal, creating vulnerability around border crossings, transit routes, and regional political disputes.

frictionVectors.title: Galamsey and mining governance
frictionVectors.details: Illegal small-scale gold mining continues to damage water systems and challenge state authority, while Accra seeks tighter control over gold purchasing, licensing, and foreign participation.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and processing terms
frictionVectors.details: Ghana is pressing for local value addition in lithium and other minerals, but financing needs and investor pressure could dilute domestic processing and revenue ambitions.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou foreign-control risk
frictionVectors.details: The Simandou iron-ore corridor is attracting major Chinese and international capital, while Guinea must balance infrastructure benefits against long-term dependence on external operators and export logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Authoritarian resource bargaining
frictionVectors.details: The military-led government is using mining concessions and infrastructure deals to strengthen its position, increasing uncertainty over contract transparency, local benefits, and political transition.

frictionVectors.title: Cashew trade dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign buyers and processors capture substantial value from Guinea-Bissau's cashew economy, while weak state capacity limits the country's ability to regulate exports and develop domestic processing.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal fishing and maritime insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Limited patrol capacity leaves coastal fisheries vulnerable to foreign fleets and illegal activity, compounded by political instability and suspected transnational trafficking networks.

frictionVectors.title: EXTERNAL DEBT AND INFRASTRUCTURE LEVERAGE
frictionVectors.details: Debt-servicing demands and reliance on multilateral lenders constrain Nairobi's fiscal autonomy. Chinese-financed transport infrastructure remains economically important, while renegotiation and repayment politics continue to shape strategic choices.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND LOGISTICS COMPETITION
frictionVectors.details: Mombasa is central to regional trade, but competition from Tanzania and pressure over logistics concessions expose Kenya to external commercial leverage. The government is balancing foreign investment with demands for tighter national control of strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: HIGHLANDS WATER PROJECT DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Water exports to South Africa provide vital revenue but leave Lesotho dependent on Pretoria for payments, infrastructure coordination, and downstream market access. Delays and cost disputes can quickly become bilateral sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: TEXTILE AND LABOR MARKET EXPOSURE
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's export manufacturing remains vulnerable to external trade preferences and foreign-owned supply chains. Changes in United States market access or regional labor conditions could weaken domestic bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION DEPENDENCE
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, gold, and other resource projects are largely structured around foreign capital and concession agreements, limiting Liberia's ability to capture value domestically. Governance capacity and contract transparency remain central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: PORT AND CORRIDOR INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: Monrovia and mineral-export corridors attract competing foreign commercial and strategic interests. Liberia must secure infrastructure investment without allowing port operations or transport networks to become instruments of external political leverage.

frictionVectors.title: DIVIDED CONTROL OF OIL ASSETS
frictionVectors.details: Rival political and security authorities continue to contest control over oil facilities, export routes, and revenue distribution. Production interruptions and shutdown threats give armed factions disproportionate leverage over the national economy.

frictionVectors.title: FOREIGN MILITARY AND ENERGY INFLUENCE
frictionVectors.details: External states and foreign security actors retain influence through military partnerships, arms networks, and energy interests. This limits the ability of Libyan institutions to establish unified control over territory and strategic infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: MINING CONCESSION IMBALANCE
frictionVectors.details: Nickel, cobalt, ilmenite, graphite, and other minerals are developed mainly through foreign-backed projects, creating jobs and export revenue but leaving Madagascar exposed to external pricing and financing conditions. Local value addition remains limited.

frictionVectors.title: INFRASTRUCTURE AND LAND CONFLICT
frictionVectors.details: Mining, transport, and energy projects frequently generate disputes over land access, environmental damage, and compensation. Weak state enforcement can allow companies or foreign financiers to shape local development terms more than national institutions do.

highlights: Debt and fuel dependence constrain autonomy

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and value capture
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-backed interests are positioning around uranium, graphite and rare-earth projects, while Malawi has limited capacity to enforce local processing and revenue safeguards.

frictionVectors.title: Fuel and infrastructure vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-exchange shortages and reliance on imported fuel leave transport and power systems exposed to external lenders, suppliers and currency conditions.

highlights: Junta tightens control over gold sector
Russian security ties replace Western influence

frictionVectors.title: Mining-code confrontation
frictionVectors.details: The state is pressing foreign mining firms for larger shares and greater operational control, increasing legal and commercial tensions with major gold producers.

frictionVectors.title: Security dependence and sanctions exposure
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on Russian security support and the Alliance of Sahel States reduces Western leverage but exposes Mali to diplomatic isolation, financing constraints and regional instability.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore gas partnership dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project with Senegal and international operators offers new revenue, but production timing, cross-border governance and revenue-sharing remain sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Mining corridors and local benefit pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign capital remains central to iron-ore expansion and rail infrastructure, creating recurring tensions over labor rights, environmental costs and domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Diego Garcia strategic bargain
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius's sovereignty claim over the Chagos Archipelago intersects with the continued strategic role of the Diego Garcia base, making implementation and access arrangements geopolitically delicate.

frictionVectors.title: Port and digital-infrastructure competition
frictionVectors.details: India, China and Western partners compete for influence in logistics, telecommunications and maritime services, requiring Mauritius to preserve regulatory autonomy and debt discipline.

highlights: Phosphate and renewables reinforce state leverage

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara resource legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Phosphate, fisheries and renewable-energy activity in Western Sahara generate diplomatic and legal pressure from Algeria, Polisario representatives and international advocacy groups.

frictionVectors.title: External infrastructure balancing
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is leveraging European, Gulf, Chinese and U.S. capital for ports, energy and industrial corridors while managing concerns over strategic dependence and regional rivalry.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled LNG Corridor
frictionVectors.details: Major gas projects depend on foreign operators, external financing, and security support, limiting Maputo's near-term leverage over revenues and infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Northern Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Militant violence in Cabo Delgado continues to threaten communities, gas facilities, transport links, and the state's effective control over resource-producing territory.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Dominates New Energy
frictionVectors.details: Offshore oil discoveries and green-hydrogen projects require substantial foreign technology and financing, creating future bargaining risks over taxation, ownership, and local value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Land Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Large energy and mining developments face pressure over scarce water, coastal ecosystems, communal land, and whether projects generate sufficient domestic employment.

frictionVectors.title: Uranium and Mining Disputes
frictionVectors.details: Niamey's push to renegotiate foreign mining arrangements strengthens political control but risks investment losses, legal disputes, and reduced technical capacity.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The shift away from French and U.S. security partnerships toward Russian support increases regime autonomy while exposing critical infrastructure and border security to a new external dependency.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Production Insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Oil theft, vandalism, and militant activity continue to reduce state control over production corridors and weaken public revenue despite sector reforms.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Retrenchment
frictionVectors.details: International majors are reducing exposure to onshore assets while retaining strategic offshore interests, leaving Nigeria to attract new financing and technical capacity on less favorable terms.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's regional influence and alleged links to mineral flows from eastern DRC generate sustained pressure over traceability, sanctions exposure, and sovereignty disputes.

frictionVectors.title: External Aid and Security Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Kigali retains strong domestic control but remains exposed to donor conditionality, diplomatic pressure, and dependence on external markets and security partnerships.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Exploration
frictionVectors.details: International firms remain interested in offshore blocks, but limited state capacity and uncertain commercial prospects constrain São Tomé and Príncipe's bargaining power. Maritime surveillance and licensing transparency are central sovereignty concerns.

frictionVectors.title: External Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The country relies heavily on foreign financing and partners for ports, energy, and digital connectivity. Competition among Chinese, European, and other external actors creates leverage but also debt and strategic-dependence risks.

frictionVectors.title: Oil and Gas Contract Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The government is pressing for greater national participation and improved terms in the Sangomar oil and Greater Tortue Ahmeyim gas projects. Tensions with international operators could affect investment confidence, production schedules, and revenue expectations.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Infrastructure Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Heavy borrowing and fiscal pressures limit Dakar's room to direct resource revenues toward domestic priorities. Ports, rail, and energy infrastructure remain dependent on foreign capital and contractors.

frictionVectors.title: EEZ Fisheries Control
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles has strong incentives to protect tuna stocks and expand marine conservation, but enforcement across its vast exclusive economic zone remains costly. Foreign fleets and licensing arrangements can dilute domestic control over marine resources.

frictionVectors.title: Indian Ocean Infrastructure Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port, coast-guard, and maritime-surveillance cooperation draws interest from India, China, and Western partners. Victoria seeks investment without allowing strategic facilities or debt exposure to compromise its non-aligned posture.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Mining Dominance
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and other mineral projects remain vital for exports but leave the state exposed to foreign operators, commodity cycles, and uneven value capture. Contract terms, local processing, and environmental enforcement are persistent sovereignty issues.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure Financing Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Power generation, roads, ports, and logistics require sustained external financing and technical support. Chinese and other foreign-backed projects provide capacity while increasing negotiation and repayment pressures.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing and Security
frictionVectors.details: Oil exploration offers potential fiscal autonomy but is constrained by limited regulatory capacity, disputed federal-state authority, and insecurity. Foreign operators and security partners will likely capture substantial early value unless institutions strengthen.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, Gulf states, China, and Western actors compete for influence through port access, security assistance, and logistics investments. Rival arrangements involving Mogadishu, Puntland, and Somaliland risk deepening fragmentation and weakening unified control of maritime assets.

highlights: Power and logistics remain strategic bottlenecks

frictionVectors.title: Foreign competition for critical minerals
frictionVectors.details: The United States, China, the European Union and Gulf investors are competing for access to South Africa's platinum-group metals, manganese and other battery inputs. Pretoria is seeking local beneficiation while avoiding excessive dependence on any single external partner.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight infrastructure weakness
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port constraints continue to reduce domestic control over mineral value chains. Private investment and external financing are increasingly important, creating leverage for foreign firms and lenders.

frictionVectors.title: Oil export dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan's fiscal survival depends on oil routed through Sudan, leaving production and revenue exposed to conflict, pipeline disruption and bargaining by external operators. Chinese and regional commercial interests remain central to the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Regional security leverage
frictionVectors.details: Unresolved political tensions and armed violence allow neighboring states and outside security actors to shape transport, trade and humanitarian access. Weak institutions limit the government's ability to convert resource rents into sovereign infrastructure.

highlights: Gold and ports draw competing patrons

frictionVectors.title: Gold economy and armed control
frictionVectors.details: Gold production and smuggling finance rival armed networks while attracting regional buyers and foreign intermediaries. The conflict has sharply reduced civilian control over extraction, taxation and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea infrastructure contest
frictionVectors.details: Port access, maritime logistics and prospective agricultural corridors are becoming bargaining assets for regional powers. External military, financial and commercial relationships risk entrenching fragmentation rather than restoring national control.

highlights: Resource nationalism paired with investment pragmatism
LNG and rail corridors define leverage

frictionVectors.title: LNG project sovereignty
frictionVectors.details: Negotiations over the long-delayed LNG development in Lindi remain a test of Tanzania's ability to secure local benefits, fiscal control and environmental safeguards while attracting international capital. The project also increases competition among Asian, European and Gulf investors.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic transport corridors
frictionVectors.details: The Central Corridor and proposed mineral-export routes are drawing external financing and regional competition. Tanzania is expanding its negotiating leverage, but debt exposure and reliance on foreign contractors remain concerns.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Port of Lomé gives Togo strategic influence over Sahel trade, but its expansion depends heavily on foreign shipping, logistics and financing networks. Regional instability increases both the port's leverage and its exposure to external security interests.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate value-chain control
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a core national asset, yet processing capacity, investment and market access are constrained by external technology and capital. Limited downstream industrialization reduces the state's ability to capture full resource value.

frictionVectors.title: EU Conditionality
frictionVectors.details: European financial support and migration cooperation give the EU significant leverage over Tunisian policy. Domestic resistance remains strong toward arrangements perceived as outsourcing border control.

frictionVectors.title: Energy and Phosphate Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Declining domestic energy output and underperforming phosphate production constrain fiscal sovereignty. Tunisia remains exposed to imported fuel costs and external financing conditions.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Transit Risk
frictionVectors.details: The East African Crude Oil Pipeline deepens Uganda's dependence on foreign capital, contractors, and Tanzanian transit infrastructure. Environmental opposition and financing restrictions continue to raise delivery and sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, Turkish, and Gulf-linked firms compete for transport, energy, and construction projects. These partnerships expand infrastructure access while increasing long-term exposure to externally controlled finance and procurement.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Ownership
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is seeking greater domestic value capture from copper and cobalt as global demand rises. Foreign mining capital remains indispensable, limiting Lusaka's bargaining power over contracts, taxation, and processing.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Corridor Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring has improved fiscal space but continues to constrain policy autonomy. Reliance on regional rail, road, and port corridors leaves mineral exports vulnerable to external infrastructure bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Battery Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese firms dominate major lithium investments, refining capacity, and export channels. Government beneficiation rules seek more local value capture but enforcement and financing remain uneven.

frictionVectors.title: Sanctions and Financial Isolation
frictionVectors.details: Western sanctions and restricted access to international finance limit infrastructure renewal and force greater reliance on non-Western partners. This narrows Zimbabwe's negotiating options and strengthens creditor and investor leverage.
